The result shows that the imine content stays at a consistently low level throughout the electrochemical reaction with a general decreasing trend, suggesting the reductive coupling between HMF and methylamine is an electrocatalytic process that occurs at the surface of the electrode.

Regarding control experiments with different metal electrodes, we have performed a comprehensive comparison. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 1, we evaluated various commercial metal foils (Fe, Ni, Cu, Pt, Zn, Sn, Ag, Cd, and In) for the electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine. These initial screening experiments clearly demonstrated that Ag exhibits exceptional electrocatalytic performance, achieving the highest partial current density and Faradaic efficiency for MAMF production among the tested metals. This superior performance was attributed to the moderate HMF adsorption strength on Ag, which is a critical finding that guided our subsequent in-depth study focusing on facet-controlled Ag catalysts and their impact on the adsorption configuration of the substrate.
Furthermore, we have conducted kinetic isotope effect (KIE) analyses on the Ag NP catalyst, as presented in Fig. 3d. The observed cathodic shift of 145 mV when replacing H O with D O strongly indicates that a proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) step is essential for the C–N coupling reaction. This analysis underscores the important role of proton dynamics in the reduction of the aldimine intermediate and C–N bond formation, providing mechanistic insight into the rate-determining step and solidifying the inner-sphere mechanism proposed in our manuscript. Due to the limitations of the experimental conditions, KIE analyses with other substrates could not be conducted in our lab. We are sorry for the unfeasible of the corresponding experiments. Specific Comment R1-3: The obvious difference between Figure 4c and Figure 4d is puzzling. Even if there are differences in the dominant adsorption configurations on the catalyst surface, it does not mean that other adsorption configurations do not exist. However, we could not observe any signals around ~1024 cm–1 which could be attributed to the furan ring of C-H, we recommend that the authors clarify this issue clearly.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments. The distinct differences between the in situ Raman spectra of Ag NP (Fig. 4c) and Ag NC (Fig. 4d) are important and serve as direct spectroscopic evidence supporting our proposed facet-dependent adsorption configurations of HMF. As stated in our manuscript, for Ag NP, the peak at 1022 cm–1 is consistently observed and attributed to the C–H stretching of the furan ring (Fig. 4a). This spectral feature is indicative of the η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration, where the furan ring adopts a horizontally tilted orientation relative to the catalyst surface, allowing for the detection of its C–H vibrations. This peak remains visible across the investigated potential range in Fig. 4c. In contrast, for Ag NC, the Raman spectra (Fig. 4d) exhibit a prominent peak at 1002 cm–1, which we attribute to the hydroxymethyl group, and the appearance of a peak at 718 cm–1 corresponding to the C–O–C stretching of the furan ring. Concurrently, the furan ring C–H stretching peak around ~1022/1024 cm–1 is indeed absent or significantly diminished on Ag NC. This distinct spectral profile on Ag NC strongly supports the η2(C,O)-aldehyde adsorption configuration. In this mode, the C–O–C end of the furan ring, along with the hydroxymethyl group, interacts more closely with the catalyst surface. This different orientation of the furan ring, where it is less horizontally oriented or more directly interacting through its oxygen-containing functionalities, would naturally lead to a reduced signal from the furan ring C–H stretching, as its vibrational mode might be less enhanced by surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) or its orientation is less favorable for detection compared to other interacting groups.
While it is plausible that other minor adsorption configurations might coexist, the dominant and distinct adsorption modes on Ag NP and Ag NC, as unequivocally evidenced by these clear and reproducible spectroscopic differences, are responsible for dictating the observed dramatic differences in reaction selectivity. The consistent correlation between these unique spectral fingerprints and the vastly different product distributions (high MAMF selectivity on Ag NP vs. favoring BHMF/BHH on Ag NC) strongly supports our conclusion that the adsorption configuration is the critical factor steering the reaction pathway. Specific Comment R1-7: Substrate Scope Expansion: Additional substrate screening experiments are necessary to validate the universality of their design strategy for aldehyde-based C–N coupling reactions. Testing structurally diverse aldehydes would clarify whether the observed mechanism is generalizable.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments. The study of the reaction between HMF and methylamine was driven by the high added value of its corresponding amine product, 5-[(methylamino)methyl]-2-furanmethanol (MAMF), which serves as a key chemical for the synthesis of the pharmaceutical Ranitidine. This consideration was stated in the Introduction section.
While we acknowledge the high utility and value of other aldehyde-based C–N coupling reactions, the current work focuses on the fundamental mechanistic insights of adsorption engineering of reactants for selective C–N coupling. Our findings establish that controlling the HMF adsorption mode (η1(C)-aldehyde vs. η2(C,O)-aldehyde) is critical for favoring C–N coupling. We believe tuning the absorption behavior should be a universal strategy for promoting heterogeneous electrochemical C–N coupling reactions. However, this universality might not be proved by testing the catalytic performance using the Ag NP and Ag NC catalysts in this work with varied aldehyde or amine substrates. The adsorption configuration tuning should be achieved by specifically designing the electrocatalyst for the target substrate. For a reaction of interest, we need to analyze the features of the substrate molecule (such as the existence of aromatic ring, the length of the alkyl chain, etc) to guide the fabrication of a specific catalyst structure, which requires a series of systematic investigations. Such a proof might be out of the scope of our current work. We will conduct related studies to further verify the effectiveness of adsorption tuning for electrochemical organic synthesis. To emphasize this point, we have added the related discussion on the future direction in the revised manuscript.

Specific Comment R2-5: The authors present a comparison of linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves for the C-N coupling and HMF reduction reactions on Ag NPs (Supplementary Fig. 14). However, the corresponding data for Ag NCs are missing. Including this comparison would provide a more complete picture of the performance differences between the two catalysts.

We agree that including the corresponding linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves for Ag NCs, comparing the C–N coupling reaction (with HMF and methylamine) and the background HMF reduction or hydrogen evolution reaction (without HMF), would provide a more complete and direct comparison of the electrochemical behavior of the two catalysts. Therefore, the results were collected and presented in Fig 2a and Supplementary Fig. 13. The results indicate that the C–N coupling reaction exhibits a lower onset potential compared to the hydrogenation of HMF. However, as the applied potential becomes increasingly negative, the HMF reduction reaction consistently shows a larger current density. This kinetic preference for HMF reduction on Ag NC is in perfect agreement with our overall findings that Ag NC favors side reactions, particularly hydrogenation (BHMF), due to its distinct η2(C,O)-aldehyde adsorption configuration. This further supports our mechanistic proposal that the specific adsorption mode on Ag NC leads to an activation of the C=O bond that is more prone to direct reduction rather than nucleophilic attack by methylamine, thereby explaining the lower C–N coupling selectivity observed on Ag NC. The explanation of this section and our revision of the manuscript are as follows:

Specific Comment R3-2: The introduction lacks a focused discussion on recent advances in electrochemical C–N coupling, particularly for biomass-derived substrates. Manuscript Lines 59-76:
Many electrocatalysts have been investigated for this reaction (Pt, Cu, Sn, Zn, and Ag).9,11
However, a lack of rational catalyst design has resulted in the easy occurrence of side reactions and low selectivity of C–N coupling12,13. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that promoting the nucleophilic attack step is crucial for effectively enhancing the overall selectivity of C–N coupling reactions11,14. Taking the electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF and methylamine as an example, the reaction pathway involves multiple steps (Scheme 1).3,11 Typically, HMF can be activated by the catalyst, forming the absorbed HMF (HMF*).9,15 Then, the target product MAMF is synthesized through two key steps16-18: (1) nucleophilic addition reaction of methylamine with the carbonyl group of HMF* to form the aldimine intermediate, and (2) subsequent reduction of the aldimine with protons from the electrolyte and electrons from the electrode to produce the MAMF (Scheme 1a). However, the hydrogenation and dimerization of HMF compete with the desired C–N coupling reaction to form 2,5-bis(hydroxymethyl)furan (BHMF) and bis(hydroxymethyl)hydrofuroin (BHH), respectively, leading to low selectivity (Scheme 1b, c).19-21 Therefore, precisely modulating the reactivity of the target aldehyde carbonyl group to facilitate nucleophilic attack becomes a key strategy for improving the selectivity of electrochemical C–N coupling.

The η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration of HMF on Ag NP appropriately promotes the polarization of the C=O bond, thereby facilitating the nucleophilic attack by methylamine and enhancing the overall selectivity of the C–N coupling reaction. The dramatic differences in product distribution and selectivity observed between Ag NP and Ag NC (Fig. 2b, c) further corroborate this surface-mediated activation. This distinct catalytic behavior strongly supports that the catalyst surface actively steers the reaction pathway by modulating HMF adsorption. Computational setup and methods.
Density functional theory methods. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed utilizing the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) in conjunction with the projector augmented wave (PAW) method.1, 2 The revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE)3 exchange-correlation functional was applied and the dispersion effects were accounted by employing semi-empirical D3 method.4, 5 For this method, the consideration of a Hubbard U parameter is typically not necessary. The cutoff energy was set to 450 eV. The convergence threshold of electronic and force was set to 10−6 eV atom–1 and 0.02 eV Å–1, respectively. The Methfessel-Paxton smearing was applied with a smearing width of 0.15 eV.
Computational model. Ag(111) and Ag(100) surface was modeled by a (3√3×3√3)R30° supercell and a 6×5 supercell, respectively. All surface models were composed of 4 layers atoms with 2 uppermost layers relaxed. The metal slabs were separated by a ~20 Å vacuum space. The Brillouin zone was sampled at a 3×3×1 k-point mesh with Γ-centered for hexagonal supercells and Monkhorst Pack for orthorhombic supercells. The Gibbs free energy under ambient conditions was corrected using a computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model.6

Specific Comment R3-7: The proposed mechanism assumes direct nucleophilic attack by methylamine on adsorbed HMF but does not address the role of protonation states or pH effects. Experiments varying pH could elucidate how proton availability impacts aldimine formation and reduction.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We chose pH 11 for the reaction electrolyte because at this pH (which is above the pKa of methylamine, ~10.6), a significant portion of methylamine is present in its neutral, nucleophilic form (CH NH ), which is essential for its efficient nucleophilic attack on the HMF carbonyl group to form the aldimine intermediate. This optimized pH condition ensures the availability of the active nucleophile.
Furthermore, our kinetic isotope effect (KIE) studies (Fig. 3d) provide direct evidence for the involvement of protons in the reaction mechanism. The observed cathodic shift of 145 mV upon switching from H O to D O strongly indicates that a proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) step is significant for the C–N coupling reaction. This confirms the important role of proton dynamics in the reduction of the aldimine intermediate and the overall C–N bond formation, thus addressing the involvement of proton availability in our proposed inner-sphere mechanism.
While systematic experiments varying pH across a wider range could indeed provide further detailed insights into how proton availability specifically impacts aldimine formation and subsequent reduction, our current study primarily focuses on elucidating the pivotal role of HMF adsorption configurations in steering reaction selectivity at an optimized pH. Exploring the full pH dependence is a valuable and logical direction for future research to further refine the understanding of the complex interplay between surface adsorption, electron transfer, and proton dynamics. The explanation of this section and our revision of the manuscript are as follows:
Manuscript Lines 412-414:
Since the pK of CH NH + is about 10.6, adjusting the solution pH to 11 ensures a significant portion of the amine to present as a base form to react with HMF to form aldimine.
Manuscript Lines 204-208:
Furthermore, electrochemical experiments with H/D kinetic isotope effect (KIE) studies were conducted on the Ag NP catalyst. The cathodic shift of 145 mV (Fig. 3d) suggests that the proton-coupled electron transfer step is significant for the C–N coupling reaction, indicating the important role of proton dynamics in the reduction of the HMF intermediate and C–N bond formation.

Specific Comment R3-8: The manuscript does not consider potential surface reconstruction of Ag NPs/NCs under operating conditions. XPS or post-reaction TEM of used catalysts would verify structural stability and rule out facet restructuring during electrolysis. Competitive adsorption between HMF and methylamine is ignored. Surface coverage studies (e.g., via electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance) could clarify whether methylamine adsorption limits reaction rates.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the important comments. Regarding potential surface reconstruction of Ag NP/NC under operating conditions, we have addressed this critical aspect with abundant experiments. As detailed in the “Result and Discussion” section and supported by Supplementary Figures 16–17, we performed post-reaction morphological and crystallographic characterization (TEM and XRD) of the used catalysts after 10 cycles of electrolysis. These results conclusively demonstrate that the morphology and crystal structure, including the predominant exposed facets, of both Ag NP and Ag NC remain almost unchanged. This robust structural stability under operando conditions ensures that the observed facet-dependent catalytic performance and selectivity are genuinely attributable to the intrinsic properties of the as-synthesized crystal facets rather than dynamic reconstruction.
Additionally, regarding the competitive adsorption behavior of substrates, our systematic optimization of methylamine concentration (to 1000 mM) ensures its abundant supply, and in situ Raman spectroscopy (Supplementary Figure 21, response to Specific Comment R3-5) confirms its stable adsorption on the catalyst surface. Furthermore, our HMF concentration dependence study (Figure 3f) indicates that HMF adsorption is a key limiting factor at lower concentrations, following Langmuir-Hinshelwood kinetics. These findings collectively suggest that under our optimized conditions, methylamine adsorption is not the rate-limiting step, and the primary kinetic and selectivity control stems from the activation and adsorption configuration of HMF. While techniques like electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM) could offer further quantitative insights into surface coverage, we could not conduct this experiment due to the limitations of the resources. It would be a valuable direction for more in-depth kinetic studies in the future, building upon the fundamental mechanistic understanding established in this work.

Specific Comment R3-9: The use of a three-electrode H-cell with a bipolar membrane may not reflect industrially relevant conditions. Testing in a flow cell or membrane electrode assembly (MEA) would better demonstrate scalability.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the beneficial comments. We agree with the reviewer that a three-electrode H-cell setup may not directly reflect industrially relevant conditions or demonstrate immediate scalability. However, it is important to emphasize that the primary objective of this fundamental research is to elucidate the intricate reaction mechanism of electrochemical C–N coupling, particularly the pivotal role of substrate adsorption configurations. Indeed, we have already performed preliminary investigations into the electrocatalytic C–N coupling reaction in a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) setup, utilizing the same reaction conditions but at higher HMF substrate concentrations (Fig. R2a). Our activity test results from the MEA system indicate a significant enhancement in reaction current and rate, primarily due to the reduced resistance afforded by the thin liquid film within the MEA, which effectively lowers the ohmic drop (Fig. R2b). However, we observed a decrease in reaction selectivity under these high substrate concentration conditions in the MEA, which we attribute to limitations in the current catalyst design when operating at such elevated concentrations and current densities.
This observation highlights a new set of challenges that require further catalyst engineering specific to MEA operation. Consequently, we have dedicated another work (Chem. Eng. Sci., 317, 122039) specifically to the study of electrocatalytic C–N coupling reactions within membrane electrode reactors. In that work, we are focusing on introducing modifications, such as the incorporation of Ru, to enhance the adsorption and activation of imine intermediates, thereby aiming to establish a robust electrocatalytic C–N coupling system capable of operating efficiently under high substrate concentrations and high current densities (Fig R2c). Therefore, while demonstrating scalability in MEA is undoubtedly crucial for the eventual practical application, the current manuscript remains focused on providing the fundamental mechanistic understanding of adsorption engineering in the H-cell, which serves as the essential groundwork for future advancements in MEA-based systems. Our subsequent work directly addresses the scalability and high-concentration challenges in MEA, building upon the mechanistic insights gained from this study. We have added the related discussion on the future direction in the revised manuscript.
Fig. R2 Electrocatalytic C–N coupling reaction between HMF and methylamine in a membrane electrode assembly (a) Conversion of HMF and selectivity of MAMF for Ag NP with varying loadings in MEA under HMF concentration of 0.1 M and current density of 80 mA cm⁻2. (b) Conversion of HMF and selectivity of MAMF in MEA on Ag NP. (c) Schematic illustration of the effective modulation of substrate adsorption configurations by Ag NP and the synergistic enhancement of imine intermediate adsorption by Ru.
Manuscript Lines 367-370:
Future efforts should focus on enabling green substrates, creating pathways to more valuable products, and designing scalable systems like the membrane electrode assembly (MEA), which will collectively pave the way for the industrial deployment of electrochemical C–N coupling technology.

Specific Comment R3-10: The environmental impact of using methylamine (a toxic reagent) is not addressed. Exploring greener amine sources (e.g., ammonia) or coupling with renewable NH₃ synthesis could enhance sustainability.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the meaningful comments. Our selection of methylamine as the nitrogen source in this study was primarily driven by the high added value of the target product, 5-[(methylamino)methyl]-2-furanmethanol (MAMF), which is a key intermediate for the synthesis of the pharmaceutical Ranitidine. This specific application highlights a direct pathway to a high-value chemical from biomass. Our current work focuses on establishing the fundamental mechanistic principles of adsorption engineering for selective C–N coupling. While exploring greener and more sustainable amine sources, such as aqueous ammonia or even coupling with electrochemical ammonia synthesis from renewable feedstocks, represents a highly significant and promising direction for future research. A key challenge with using ammonia as an N source is the difficulty in selectively obtaining specific primary or secondary amine products. This would undoubtedly enhance the overall sustainability profile of electrochemical C–N coupling processes, and is a direction we are committed to investigating in our future work. We have added the related discussion on the future direction in the revised manuscript.

### Reviewer 1

In reviewing the responses, we note that the authors are trying to improve their work and have corrected several issues. However, our major concerns remain unresolved. We still hold the view that the authors seem to be insufficiently informed regarding the issues we highlighted in our previous comment. Moreover, the revisions to the mechanistic discussion and theoretical calculations lack justification, which is highly irresponsible and further exacerbates our concerns regarding the reliability of the data. The following comments should be taken for more consideration.
1. The authors emphasize that the difference in exposed crystal facets between Ag NPs and Ag NCs is key to altering selectivity, suggesting that the (111) facet dominates the high selectivity in hydrogenation reactions. However, due to facet heterogeneity, we believe that this interpretation overstates the data. The potential contribution of the (200) facet, or even involvement of the (220) facet, cannot be ruled out. Furthermore, synergistic effects between different crystal facets may also play a role. Clearly, attributing the regulation of selectivity solely to a single facet is unreasonable.
2. The authors propose that the adsorption pattern of furan on the Ag surface is critical for selectivity. However, the current experimental evidence may not sufficiently support this claim. Therefore, we believe the authors should expand the substrate scope and verify the generality of their proposed synthetic strategy, particularly by exploring furan-related structures.
3. Regarding the experiment tracking intermediates via 1H NMR, we find the results puzzling. If the imine is a key intermediate, its concentration should remain relatively stable during continuous generations. The authors need to explain this observation.
4. Additionally, concerning the imine intermediate, we suggest that the authors should directly use it as a reactant in electrocatalytic selective reduction to validate the mechanism. We are particularly concerned about whether this species can remain stable under alkaline electrolytic conditions.
5. Furthermore, the central challenge of this reaction remains unclear. While the authors assert that controlling selectivity is a major obstacle in the direct reduction process, this issue would be bypassed by using the pre-synthesized imine as the substrate. Moreover, the formation of the imine itself does not appear difficult, and the authors acknowledge its spontaneous formation under specific conditions. Hence, the significance of this study remains unclear to us.
The authors should address the aforementioned questions seriously and directly and persuade me about the reliability and validity of all the data. Additionally, the findings presented here starkly diverge from the rigorous expectations and stringent standards that are synonymous with the high-impact, prestigious Nature Communications. These discrepancies underscore a significant departure from the normative benchmarks that the scientific community anticipates from publications within this esteemed domain, highlighting a need for alignment with the journal's commitment to publishing only the most groundbreaking and impactful research.

## Paper

## Abstract

The electrochemical C–N coupling of biomass-derived 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) with methylamine offers a promising sustainable route to value-added amines. However, achieving high selectivity remains challenging due to competing side reactions, including C=O hydrogenation and C–C dimerization. This paper describes tailoring the surface structure of Ag catalysts to modulate HMF adsorption and intermediate hydrogenation behavior and thus enhancing C–N coupling selectivity. Ag nanoparticles, predominantly exposing the (111) facet, exhibit higher selectivity compared with Ag nanocubes mainly enclosed by (100) planes. The Ag (111) facet favors the C–N coupling pathway by regulating both adsorption geometry and hydrogenation ability. In-situ Raman spectroscopy and density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that an η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration, dominant on Ag (111), enhances carbonyl electrophilicity and facilitates C=O polarization, promoting nucleophilic attack by methylamine. In contrast, the η2(C,O)–aldehyde configuration, more common on Ag (100), stabilizes the C=O bond, limiting its reactivity. Moreover, Ag (111) shows enhanced imine hydrogenation activity, further improving amine selectivity. This study highlights the significance of facet-dependent adsorption modulation in steering reaction pathways and advancing sustainable electrochemical synthesis.

---

## Introduction

Amines are fine chemicals extensively applied in chemical, pharmaceutical, agrochemical, and material industries1–3. Among various amines, 5-[(methylamino)methyl]−2-furanmethanol (MAMF) serves as a key chemical for the synthesis of the pharmaceutical Ranitidine4. MAMF could be fabricated by the reductive amination of HMF with methylamine5,6. However, traditional production routes often rely on hazardous reducing agents and harsh reaction conditions, leading to high energy consumption and severe side reactions4,7. Electrochemical approaches enable controlled C–N bond formation through potential modulation and catalyst design, offering sustainable MAMF synthesis under ambient conditions with electrons as clean reductants8–10.

The electro-reductive amination of HMF can proceed either via a one-step direct reaction between HMF and methylamine or through a two-step route in which HMF first undergoes spontaneous condensation with methylamine to generate an intermediate imine, followed by its electrochemical reduction on the catalyst surface. However, during reductive conditions, the local pH near the cathode rises due to hydroxide accumulation11, making the imine intermediate susceptible to hydrolysis at the interface. This hydrolytic back-reaction regenerates HMF and methylamine, rendering the two-step pathway kinetically indistinguishable from the one-step process. Moreover, the two-step approach generally requires prolonged reaction times and additional separation steps, complicating the overall synthesis12,13. Unwanted side reactions may also occur: two imine molecules can couple to form diamine species, while the primary amine product may further condense with unreacted imine to yield a secondary imine that can be subsequently hydrogenated into a secondary amine. Moreover, imines may undergo polymerization or trimerization in solutions, leading to complex product mixtures, which have been reported previously (Supplementary Fig. 1)12. Considering these factors, the one-step electrolysis strategy was adopted and systematically investigated in this work.

In addition to reaction pathways, the hydrogenation ability of catalysts could also affect the product distribution of electrocatalytic C–N coupling13–15. Insufficient hydrogenation capability hinders the timely reduction of imine intermediate, facilitating its hydrolysis back to HMF and methylamine, thereby lowering overall selectivity toward MAMF. Comparative studies in thermal reductive amination systems have demonstrated that a moderate and directional hydrogenation ability is optimal for locking the rate-determining step at the selective hydrogenation of C=N, which maximizes primary amine formation and suppresses over-hydrogenation and other side reactions16.

Before the catalyst design, different metal electrocatalysts have been investigated for this reaction (Pt, Cu, Sn, Zn, and Ag)9,17. However, a lack of rational catalyst design has resulted in the easy occurrence of side reactions and low selectivity of C–N coupling18,19. To overcome these performance limitations, it is essential to understand the reaction from a mechanistic perspective. Previous studies have shown that enhancing the nucleophilic attack step is critical for effectively improving the overall selectivity of electrochemical C–N coupling reactions9,17. Taking the electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF and methylamine as an example, the reaction pathway involves multiple steps (Fig. 1)3,17. Typically, HMF could be activated by the catalyst, forming the absorbed HMF (HMF*)9,12. Then, the target product MAMF could be synthesized through two key steps13–15: (1) nucleophilic addition reaction of methylamine with the carbonyl group of HMF* to form the aldimine intermediate, and (2) subsequent reduction of the aldimine with protons from the electrolyte and electrons from the electrode to produce the MAMF (Fig. 1a). However, the hydrogenation and dimerization of HMF would compete with the desired C–N coupling reaction to form 2,5-bis(hydroxymethyl)furan (BHMF) and bis(hydroxymethyl)hydrofuroin (BHH), respectively, leading to low selectivity (Fig. 1b,c)16,20,21. Therefore, precise modulation of the aldehyde carbonyl reactivity and the catalyst’s hydrogenation ability to facilitate nucleophilic attack and subsequent imine conversion could be a useful strategy for enhancing the selectivity of electrochemical C–N coupling.

Tuning the adsorption behaviors of substrates on the catalyst surface has been proven essential for changing the electrochemical reaction pathways22,23. For example, the adsorption configuration of HMF is different on various metal electrodes, affecting the elongation of the aldehyde C=O bond, which impacts the reaction pathways24,25. This phenomenon provides a general idea of improving the selectivity of C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine by designing catalysts with appropriate substrate absorption configuration26–28. Adjusting the hydrogenation ability of the intermediate could further affect the product distribution. Among different catalyst design strategies29–31, facet engineering could precisely control substrate adsorption configurations and hydrogenation owing to the specific atomic arrangements and electronic structures of a certain facet32,33. For example, Koper et al. revealed that facet-dependent adsorption configurations of organic ketones govern electrochemical reduction selectivity on Pt surfaces34. Acetophenone was horizontally adsorbed on Pt(111) with the compacted adsorption of the phenyl ring, enhancing carbonyl reduction. In contrast, the vertical adsorption configuration of 4-acetylpyridine on Pt(100) increases the distance between the carbonyl functional group and the catalyst surface, thereby suppressing reduction activity compared to acetophenone. Therefore, these facet-dependent adsorption effects highlight a general structure-selectivity relationship, underscoring that a mechanistic understanding of how adsorption configurations govern intermediate activation and hydrogenation is essential for rationally designing catalysts with improved selectivity for the electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine.

In this work, Ag catalysts with well-defined structures and preferentially exposed facets are fabricated to investigate the impact of the adsorption behaviors of substrates and hydrogenation ability of intermediates on the selectivity of the C–N coupling reaction9,35.

---

## Results

To rationalize the choice of the one-step C–N coupling pathway, comparative electrolysis experiments were conducted using an Ag foil to evaluate the selectivity between direct coupling and the two-step route via the pre-formed imine intermediate. The direct electrochemical coupling between HMF and methylamine exhibited an FE of 62.3%, significantly higher than the 39.8% obtained for the imine-mediated process. In contrast, the two-step reaction yielded a more complex product distribution (Supplementary Fig. 2), likely due to secondary condensation leading to diamine or triamine species. To further elucidate the role of adsorption properties in governing C–N coupling activity, a series of metal foils (Fe, Ni, Cu, Pt, Zn, Sn, Ag, Cd, and In) with distinct adsorption affinities toward HMF were systematically examined17. Among those metals, Ag demonstrates relatively good electrocatalytic performance in the C–N coupling reaction, achieving the highest partial current density of 13 mA cm–2 and FE of 62.3% for MAMF production due to the moderate HMF adsorption strength among tested metal foils (Supplementary Fig. 3)16,40. To further investigate the impact of adsorption behavior of HMF on the electrochemical C–N coupling, Ag NP and Ag nanocubes (Ag NC) with varied exposed facets and surface electronic structures were successfully fabricated. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images revealed that Ag NP exhibits an early spherical morphology with an average diameter of approximately 30 nm, whereas Ag NC exhibits cubic shapes (Fig. 2a, b). Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) characterization (Fig. 2c–f and Supplementary Fig. 4) further confirms that Ag NP and Ag NC exhibit distinct morphologies. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) images and the corresponding fast Fourier transform (FFT) patterns (Fig. 2d, f) provide evidence of the surface structures (Supplementary Fig. 5). Ag NP exhibits a lattice spacing of 0.24 nm, corresponding to the (111) crystallographic plane of Ag. On the other hand, Ag NC shows a lattice spacing of 0.21 nm, which corresponds to the (200) plane of Ag41. Additionally, the primary diffraction peaks in the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns confirm that Ag NP and Ag NC mainly expose the (111) and (100) facets, respectively (Fig. 2g). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) characterization (Fig. 1h) was conducted to confirm that Ag in these catalysts exists in the metallic state32,42. These results demonstrate the successful synthesis of Ag catalysts with well-controlled crystal structures.

Electrochemical activity tests for the C–N coupling reaction of HMF with methylamine were conducted in a three-electrode H-cell (Supplementary Fig. 6), using a 0.5 M phosphate buffer solution as the electrolyte (see the Methods for more details)9,12. The liquid and gaseous products were quantified by liquid chromatography (LC) and gas chromatography (GC), respectively (Supplementary Figs. 7–14). The methylamine concentration was optimized, and 1000 mM was selected according to the performance tests (Supplementary Fig. 15). Linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 16) indicate that both Ag NP and Ag NC exhibit enhanced current densities upon the addition of HMF, suggesting that the electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine requires a lower overpotential compared to the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Ag NP achieves a current density of ~20 mA cm–2 at –0.45 V vs. RHE, which is higher than that of Ag NC (~14 mA cm–2). Notably, the Ag NC exhibits a higher current density of HMF reduction as the potential becomes more negative (lower than –0.45 V), suggesting that direct HMF reduction might be more favorable on Ag NC.

Ag NP and Ag NC with different surface structures exhibit distinct selectivity and product distributions in the electrochemical C–N coupling reaction of HMF and methylamine (Fig. 3b, c). Tests at a wide range of potentials (–0.35 V to –0.75 V vs. RHE) demonstrate that Ag NP shows better performance in both selectivity and FE of electrochemical C–N coupling compared to Ag NC. The highest FE of 89.2% could be achieved by Ag NP with a selectivity of 90.2% at –0.45 V vs. RHE (Fig. 2b), which outperforms most previously reported C–N coupling systems (Supplementary Table S1)9,17–19,36. Regarding the distribution of products, Ag NC shows a higher FE of BHH than Ag NP at various voltages (Fig. 3c), with more BHH produced at low potentials (–0.35 V and –0.45 V vs. RHE). Furthermore, Ag NC exhibits a rising trend in BHMF production even in the presence of methylamine at higher potentials (–0.55 V to –0.75 V vs. RHE). These results indicate that, on Ag NCs, the aldehyde group of HMF preferentially undergoes hydrogenation to BHMF or dimerization to BHH, which is likely attributable to the strong interaction between the catalyst surface and the C=O moiety16,33,40. Additionally, introducing BHMF into the electrolyte with methylamine at reductive potentials eliminates the possibility of MAMF production from BHMF (Supplementary Fig. 17), indicating that these two reactions are competitive on Ag catalysts. Furthermore, Ag NP possesses a slightly smaller electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) than Ag NC (Supplementary Fig. 18), suggesting that Ag NP has a better intrinsic performance. Therefore, the higher production rate of MAMF on Ag NP suggests that the adsorption behavior on Ag NP favors the C–N coupling process (Fig. 3d). During stability tests, Ag NP shows the steady production of MAMF with a consistent FE (>85%) over 24 h (Fig. 3e), higher than that of the Ag NC (Fig. 3e, f). The morphology and crystal structure of the Ag catalysts remain unchanged (Supplementary Figs. 19 and 20), suggesting the importance of the exposed facet for the promoted activity. The results above indicate that the adsorption behaviors of HMF seem to be essential for selectivity. To validate the generality of our findings, we broadened the substrate scope to several furfural derivatives and varied the nitrogen source. With 2-furaldehyde and 5-methylfurfural as substrates and methylamine as the nucleophile, Ag NP delivered FEs of 63.0% and 81.0% toward the corresponding amines, whereas Ag NC afforded lower FEs of 50.4% and 69.1%, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 21a, b). Replacing methylamine with ammonia as the nitrogen source in the coupling reaction with HMF preserved a high MAMF FE of 65.3% on Ag NP, higher than that of 29.1% on Ag NC (Supplementary Fig. 21c). Taken together, these results validate a facet-governed adsorption-reactivity paradigm. The Ag NP surface favors the η1(C)-aldehyde configuration, translates into favorable product selectivity across distinct furfural substrates and nitrogen sources, indicating the versatility of facet engineering for electrochemical amination (Supplementary Fig. 21d).

To further support this hypothesis, it is necessary to elucidate the intrinsic reaction mechanism of C–N coupling and how the HMF adsorption behavior affect the performance.

To further investigate the reaction mechanism of electrochemical C–N coupling, kinetics studies were carried out on Ag catalysts. The Tafel slopes (Fig. 4a, b) for Ag NP (157 mV dec–1) and Ag NC (168 mV dec–1) are lower compared to blank counterparts of Ag NP and Ag NC (179 mV dec–1 and 182 mV dec–1). This reduction in Tafel slopes demonstrates that the electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine is kinetically more favorable than HER. Notably, the smaller Tafel slope of Ag NP than Ag NC implies more favorable kinetics of Ag NP for C–N coupling12,28,34. This result is further supported by the electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) study (Fig. 4c and Supplementary Fig. 22). The Ag NPs exhibit a reduced charge-transfer resistance (R=12.4 Ω) compared to Ag NCs (R=18.7 Ω), indicating enhanced interfacial electron transfer efficiency during the C–N coupling process43,44. Furthermore, electrochemical experiments with H/D kinetic isotope effect (KIE) studies were conducted on the Ag NP catalyst. The cathodic shift of 145 mV (Fig. 4d) suggests that the proton-coupled electron transfer step is significant for the C–N coupling reaction, indicating the important role of proton dynamics in the reduction of the HMF intermediate and C–N bond formation17,36,45,46. Besides, time-resolved 1H NMR spectroscopic characterization of the reaction mixture was performed under operando electrochemical conditions (Supplementary Fig. 23). The results show that the imine intermediate remains at a consistently low concentration throughout the electrochemical reaction, exhibiting a gradual decline as electrolysis proceeds. This behavior can be attributed to the continuous conversion and hydrolysis of the imine at the electrode–electrolyte interface, where the elevated local pH promotes hydrolytic decomposition. In contrast, the imine concentration remains nearly constant in the absence of applied potential, confirming that electrolysis induces its consumption (Supplementary Fig. 24).

According to Fick’s first law, we have calculated the local alkalinity during the reaction47. It was found that the local pH elevated to nearly 12.6 at –0.45 V vs. RHE (Supplementary Fig. 25a, see the Methods for more detials). To further verify this observation, the imine was synthesized independently and introduced into electrolyte solutions with pH 11.0 and 12.6. The imine remained relatively stable at pH 11.0 but underwent hydrolysis under pH 12.6 conditions (Supplementary Fig. 25). Considering the enhanced local alkalinity near the cathode during electrolysis, these results substantiate our rationale for adopting a one-step C–N coupling strategy and highlight the critical importance of controlling the interfacial adsorption configuration and hydrogenation ability to achieve high selectivity36,48,49.

Kinetic analysis of the reaction process shows that a decline in FE for C–N coupling correlates with the concentration decrease of HMF as consumed during electrolysis (Fig. 4e), accompanied by a rise in HER activity. This trend further supports the conclusion that the C–N coupling reaction follows the inner-sphere route17,36,45. Further validation is provided by the dependence of the MAMF partial current density on the HMF concentration. In the low-concentration regime (Fig. 4f), a logarithmic slope of 0.62 is observed, which is close to the theoretical value of 0.5 predicted by Langmuir–Hinshelwood kinetics for bimolecular surface reactions. This agreement suggests that the surface adsorption of HMF becomes a key rate-limiting factor under these conditions5,49. At higher HMF concentrations, side reactions like polymerization and reduction increase, inhibiting the C–N coupling reaction23. These findings collectively demonstrate that HMF adsorption modulated by catalyst surface properties directly affects the competition between C–N coupling and side reactions.

To clarify the adsorption behavior of HMF on Ag NP and Ag NC, spectroscopic studies were carried out. Before the in situ experiments for the C–N coupling reaction, the Raman spectra of HMF, methylamine, and possible products (MAMF and BHMF) were first collected to confirm key peaks for further experiments (Supplementary Fig. 26). Raman spectroscopy enables precise detection of adsorption-induced spectral perturbations, including frequency shifts and intensity variation, by leveraging its high sensitivity to molecular vibrational modes50. Notably, Ag NP and NC exhibit distinct spectral responses to HMF adsorption (Fig. 5a). For Ag NP, peaks at 976 cm–1 and 1526 cm–1 are attributed to the C–C stretching of the furan ring. The peak at 1022 cm–1 is attributed to the C–H stretching of the furan ring. These results show that HMF is adsorbed on Ag NP with the horizontally tilted furan ring51,52. This adsorption configuration shows that the C–C end of the furan ring is closer to the catalyst surface on Ag NP, with the absence of the peak at 718 cm–1 attributed to C–O–C stretching. For Ag NC, the appearance of the peak at 718 cm–1 and the disappearance of peaks at 976 cm–1 and 1526 cm–1 confirm that the C–O–C end of the furan ring interacts more closely with the catalyst surface53. The peak at 1002 cm–1 is attributed to the hydroxymethyl group54,55. The absence of a peak at 1526 cm–1 on Ag NC could suggest that Ag NC preferentially adsorbs the oxygen-containing bonds (C–O–C of the furan ring, C–OH of the alcohol, and C=O of the aldehyde)56. These results show that the adsorption configuration of HMF is strongly dependent on the Ag catalysts, possibly owing to the different surface structures.

The varied adsorption configurations of HMF could be further supported by the results of density functional theory (DFT) calculations (Fig. 5b). DFT results reveal that HMF preferentially adopts the η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption mode on Ag NP, where the furan ring tilts horizontally and the aldehyde group of HMF coordinates monodentate to the catalyst surface through the carbonyl carbon atom. Additionally, Ag NC stabilizes the η2(C,O)-aldehyde configuration, in which the C atom and the O atom of the carbonyl group are together bonded to the surface. These distinct adsorption modes could influence the interaction strength and orientation of the C=O group with catalytic sites57,58. Furthermore, the calculated adsorption energy difference (Fig. 5b) indicates that the thermodynamic stabilization of the η1(C)-aldehyde configuration, which concurrently improves both the activation efficiency and adsorption stability of the C=O group during prolonged electrolysis35,59. Therefore, it is proposed that the Ag catalysts affect the selectivity of the C–N coupling reaction by controlling the adsorption mode of the aldehyde group of HMF.

To further understand the mechanism of structure-influenced adsorption configurations in steering C–N coupling reaction, in situ Raman spectroscopy investigations were carried out at the potentials from –0.15 V to –0.75 V vs. RHE with an interval of 0.1 V (Fig. 5c, d). Adsorbed species on the Ag surface are observed under reduction conditions. The C–C, C–H vibrations of the furan ring observed at open circuit potential (Fig. 5c) could all be found at a similar Raman shift as those found in Fig. 4a, suggesting that HMF is adsorbed on Ag NP via η1(C)-aldehyde configuration in the electrochemical C–N coupling process. The peaks for aldehyde (1391 cm–1 and ~1670 cm–1) and furan ring (1523 cm–1) are observed from –0.15 V to –0.75 V vs. RHE, indicating a stabilized adsorption on Ag NP at a wide potential range (Fig. 5c)60. For Ag NC, peaks of HMF appear at 718 cm–1, 1002 cm–1, and 1506 cm–1, consistent with η2(C, O)-aldehyde adsorption mode (Fig. 5d). Control experiments without HMF are investigated under the same applied potential. The peak at ca. 1300 cm–1 (Supplementary Fig. 27), attributed to the wagging of –NH260,61 and stable adsorption of methylamine, eliminates the concerns about the identification of adsorption configurations and the influence of methylamine adsorption.

Upon applying the negative potential, peaks at 1452 cm–1 attributed to symmetric stretching of the C–N bond are detected at –0.15 V to –0.75 V vs. RHE, demonstrating the generation of MAMF (Supplementary Fig. 26c). The surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) effect amplifies the furan ring vibration at 1562 cm–1 in generated MAMF46, demonstrating that the reaction occurs preferentially near the Ag NP surface rather than in bulk solution. Additionally, the relatively lower intensity of the peak of the C–N bond in MAMF on Ag NC (peak at 1452 cm–1) corresponds to the lower coverage of MAMF under operando conditions25,47, implying that the reaction did not favor the C–N coupling (Fig. 5e). In particular, the vibration peak at 1589 cm–1, assigned to the hydrogenation product BHMF (Supplementary Fig. 26d), is absent in the Raman spectra of Ag NP (Fig. 5d), indicating that the η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration effectively suppresses the competing hydrogenation pathway. However, the peak of BHMF was observed on Ag NC from –0.25 V to –0.65 V vs. RHE, indicating that the C–N coupling reaction was inhibited by the hydrogenation of HMF.

The Raman peak at 1678 cm–1 attributed to the stretching mode of C=O in HMF (blue curve in Fig. 5a) shows a 3 cm–1 red shift on Ag NP (Fig. 5c)50,62. The red shift is assigned to the adsorption of HMF through the carbonyl π* antibonding orbital and indicates the weakening of C=O bond on Ag NP25,63. Compared to Ag NP, the 9 cm–1 red shift of C=O on Ag NC indicates a stronger interaction (Fig. 5d)50,53. Furthermore, the relatively larger stark tuning (Supplementary Fig. 28) of Ag NC demonstrates the excessive interaction of aldehyde53,64, leading to the cleavage of C=O to form BHH or BHMF16,28. This divergence in binding geometry directly modulates the polarization degree of the C=O group. The η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption on Ag NP induces moderate electron withdrawal from the carbonyl moiety compared to the η2(C, O)-aldehyde adsorption on Ag NC, thereby enhancing its susceptibility to nucleophilic attack by absorbed methylamine (Fig. 1a) rather than the hydrogenation (Fig. 1b) and dimerization (Fig. 1c)16,26.

To further exclude how the adsorption configuration affects the selectivity, DFT calculations were carried out. The results reveal that the nucleophilic attack of methylamine on adsorbed HMF over Ag NP exhibits a Gibbs free energy barrier of –0.28 eV that is lower than –0.14 eV on Ag NC. Considering potential contribution from the trace facet of (110), the C–N coupling energy barrier on Ag (110) was also considered. It showed that the C–N coupling energy barrier is –0.17 eV, higher than that on Ag (111). The hydrogenation barrier of the imine is also calculated. Ag (111) surface exhibits the lowest hydrogenation energy barrier (0.07 eV), markedly lower than those on Ag (100) (0.24 eV) and Ag (110) (0.13 eV). Such a low barrier facilitates the rapid hydrogenation of the imine intermediate, thereby accelerating the overall conversion and enhancing the C–N coupling selectivity (Supplementary Fig. 29)23,65. As a result, Ag NP stabilizes η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration with optimal interaction of C=O for C–N coupling, whereas Ag NC favors η2(C, O)-aldehyde configurations that steer reactions toward hydrogenation.

These spectroscopic and computational results highlight that the adsorption configuration of HMF could play a crucial role in affecting the selectivity of electrochemical C–N coupling. As shown in Fig. 5e, HMF tends to absorb on the Ag NP via η1(C)-aldehyde configuration. Due to the moderate adsorption strength of C=O, nucleophilic attack of methylamine would occur preferentially. Thereafter, hydrogen atom transfer (HAT) would transfer H* on the electrode to the adsorbed organic species rapidly to converting imine to respective amines48,56. The mechanism of Ag NP gives clear evidence that η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration favors generating the C–N bond and suppressing the side reactions. Furthermore, the stronger polarization of aldehyde C=O on Ag NC contributes to straight HAT to form BHH and BHMF rather than coupling with methylamine. Given the reaction pathways for C–N coupling, MAMF would not be generated once the straight HAT to aldehyde happens (Fig. 1). The specific structures of catalyst surfaces impact the C–N coupling selectivity by controlling HMF adsorption configurations and imine hydrogenation that differentially activate the C=O group for the nucleophilic attack28,62. Therefore, manipulating the adsorption configuration of HMF and the hydrogenation of imine on Ag catalysts could enhance the FE of electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine.

In this work, we rationalized the choice of a one-step C–N coupling pathway by directly comparing it with the conventional two-step process via the imine intermediate. Building on this understanding, we achieved highly efficient electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine by tailoring the adsorption configuration of HMF on Ag catalysts predominantly exposing the (111) facet. A high FE of 89.2% for MAMF with a selectivity of 90.2% could be achieved by Ag NP with exposed Ag (111) facet. Kinetics studies reveal that the C–N coupling follows an inner-sphere mechanism, where the adsorption behavior of HMF and hydrogenation of imine could play a crucial role in affecting the product distribution. In situ Raman spectroscopy and DFT calculations reveal that the η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration of HMF on Ag NP leads to an optimal interaction strength of the functional aldehyde group with the catalyst surface. Besides, the better imine hydrogenation on Ag NP further helps to convert the imine to the respective amines. Thus, the polarization of the C=O could be optimized to facilitate the C–N bond formation while suppressing side reactions such as hydrogenation and dimerization. This work offers new insights into how substrate adsorption configuration regulates the selectivity of electrochemical C–N coupling between HMF and methylamine. These findings could potentially guide the design of efficient catalysts for electrochemical organic synthesis. Future efforts should focus on enabling green substrates, creating pathways to more valuable products, and designing scalable systems like the membrane electrode assembly (MEA), which will collectively pave the way for the industrial deployment of electrochemical C–N coupling technology.
