## Methods

Materials
AgNO3 (>99.8%), methylamine (40 wt.% in H2O), and acetone (HPLC) were purchased from Tianjin Jiangtian Chemical Technology Co., Ltd. (China). 5-Hydroxymethylfurfural (99%), CF3COOAg (98%) and polyvinylpyrrolidone (PVP, Mv=55,000–58,000, 98%) were purchased from Meryer (Shanghai) Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. K2HPO4 (98%), 5-[(methylamino)methyl]-2-furanmethanol (95%), 2,5-bis(hydroxymethyl)furan (98%) were purchased from Bide Pharmatech Ltd. NaOH (99%), ethylene glycol (HPLC), acetonitrile (HPLC) and NaCl (99%) were purchased from Aladdin Industrial Co. Ltd. NaHS (68–72%), ammonium formate (>99%) were purchased from Energy Chemical (Anhui, China). Sodium citrate (>99%) was purchased from J&K Scientific Ltd. L(+)-Ascorbic acid was purchased from Tianjin Guangfu Technology Development Co. Ltd. (China). KOH (96%) was purchased from Macklin Inc. (Shanghai, China). All gases used in this paper were from Air Liquide Co. Ltd., and all reagents except 5-[(methylamino)methyl]-2-furanmethanol (MAMF) were used directly without further purification.

Synthesis of Ag NP and Ag NC
Ag NP was synthesized using L(+)-ascorbic acid as the reductant and sodium citrate anhydrous as the stabilizer. Typically, 0.23 g ascorbic acid and 0.77 g sodium citrate anhydrous were dissolved in 200 mL of deionized water, and the pH of the solution was adjusted to 11 by adding 0.1 mol L–1 NaOH solution66. Subsequently, 4 mL of 0.5 mol L–1 aqueous solution of AgNO3 was added dropwise under continuous stirring (900 rpm) in a 30°C water bath. The solution immediately changed from colorless to black, indicating the formation of Ag nanoparticles. After 150 min of reaction, the product was collected by centrifugation at 9000 rpm for 5 min, washed repeatedly with ethanol and deionized water, and finally redispersed after a second centrifugation at the same speed to obtain purified Ag NP.

In a standard synthesis for Ag NC, 25 mL of ethylene glycol (EG) was added into a flask and heated for 40 min under magnetic stirring in an oil bath set to 142°C. A stable temperature of approximately 138°C was measured for the reaction solution. Other reagents were separately dissolved in EG and sequentially introduced into the flask using a pipette. Specifically, 0.3 mL of NaHS solution (3.5 mM) was added first. After 4 min, 2.5 mL of NaCl solution (3 mM) was introduced, followed by the addition of 6.25 mL of PVP solution (20 mg mL–1) 2 min later. After another 2 min, 2 mL of CF3COOAg solution (282 mM) were introduced. Finally, 2.5 mL of NaBr solution (3 mM) was added after 5 min of delay. Note that the NaHS solution was prepared right before its injection. During the entire process, the flask was capped with a glass stopper except during the addition of reagents. After growth for 15 min, the synthesis was quenched by immersing the flask in an ice-water bath. The solution was split into four portions, and 125 mg of PVP was dissolved in each fraction. This is necessary in order to prevent aggregation during the washing steps. The products were precipitated with acetone and collected by centrifugation at 8000 rpm for 6 min, followed by washing with DI water and centrifuging at 12000 rpm for 10 min twice to remove the remaining precursor, EG, and excessive PVP67. Since the use of NaBr during the synthesis, the product solution was centrifuged twice at 9000 rpm for 10 min to separate the insoluble AgBr precipitate from the Ag NC solution.

Fabrication of electrodes
For the preparation of electrodes, 30 mg of catalyst (Ag NP or Ag NC) with 160 μL of Nafion (5 wt.%) were dispersed in 3 mL of ethanol. After 40 min of sonication in an ice water bath, the catalyst ink was sprayed onto carbon paper at a set temperature of 78°C. The loadings of the catalysts were controlled to be 1 mg cm–2.

Activity evaluation
The electrochemical performances of all the samples were tested using the AutoLAB electrochemical analyzer and carried out in an H-type cell. The anolyte (20 mL of buffer solution) and the catholyte (20 mL of buffer solution containing 20 mM HMF and methylamine) were separated by a bipolar membrane (BPM, Fumasep FBM-PK, Fumatech). Since the pKa of CH3NH3+ is about 10.6, adjusting the solution pH to 11±0.2 ensures a significant portion of the amine to present as a base form to react with HMF to form aldimine. The electrolyte was freshly prepared the same day before the experiment. The 0.5 M phosphate buffer solution was prepared by using K2HPO4 and adjusting the pH to 11.0 with KOH. And pH of the solution was monitored before (11.0±0.2) and after (11.1±0.3) adding the methylamine to make sure no obvious change was observed.

The catholyte was stirred for 10 min with Ar protection before electrolysis. Carbon rod and Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) electrodes were used as the anode and the reference electrode, respectively. The carbon paper of the working electrode was cut into a size of 2 cm2, and the geometric surface area for activity tests is 1.5 cm2. The backside of the carbon paper is covered with Kapton tape. All the tests for electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine were conducted under magnetic stirring at 1200 rpm. The electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements were performed with a 5 mV amplitude and a frequency range from 10,000 to 0.1 Hz. All the potentials in this paper were provided without iR corrected and converted to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) through the following equation:

E RHE = E Ag/AgCl + 0.197 + 0.059 × pH (1)

Product identification and quantification
During the reaction, the catholyte was continually stirred at 1200 rpm with Ar as the protective gas and carrier gas (flow rate: 5 sccm). The products were quantified after the amount of electrons flowing through the cathode reached 20 C as controlled by a potentiostat (Autolab PGSTAT204, Metrohm). Gaseous products were analyzed with online gas chromatography (GC7890B, Agilent Technologies, Inc.). For quantification of liquid products, the collected catholyte was first subjected to rotary evaporation at 40°C to remove residual methylamine. Subsequently, the obtained liquid products were diluted fivefold and analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC, Agilent Technologies 1200 Infinity) equipped with a variable wavelength detector (VWD). The products were analyzed with a C18 column. The mobile phase is acetonitrile/DI water/5% ammonium formate (V/V/V=6:1:3) solution with a flow rate of 0.5 mL min–1. The formation of products was further ensured by mass spectrometry (MS) and 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy.

The FE, selectivity and production rate are calculated according to Eqs. (2)–(6):

FE H2 = 2n H2 × F / Q × 100% (2)

FE MAMF = 2n MAMF × F / Q × 100% (3)

FE BHMF = 2n BHMF × F / Q × 100% (4)

Selectivity MAMF = n MAMF / (n0 HMF - n HMF) × 100% (5)

Production rate MAMF (mg cm–2 h–1) = m MAMF / (S catalyst × t) (6)

where the n MAMF, n BHMF and n HMF represent the mole amounts of MAMF, BHMF after the electrolysis. The n0 HMF represent the mole amount of HMF before reaction. The Y HMF represents the yield of HMF. Q refers to the total charge. F is Faraday’s constant. S catalyst is the geometric area of the catalyst loaded on the electrode, and t is the reaction time.

Characterizations
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Regulus 8100) was employed to characterize the morphology of the catalysts. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL JEM-2100F) was used to characterize the structure of the catalysts. X-ray powder diffraction (XRD; Bruker D8 Focus, Cu Kα radiation (λ=1.54056 Å) at 40 kV and 40 mA) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with an Al Kα X-ray source (XPS, EscaLab MK) were applied to characterize the structure and valence states of the as-prepared catalysts. XRD spectra were collected over a 2θ range of 10–80° at a scanning speed of 10°/min. The binding energy was calibrated using the C 1s photoelectron peak at 284.6 eV as the reference.

In situ Raman spectroscopy
In situ Raman experiments were carried out in a custom-designed H-cell electrolyzer, using 0.5 M phosphate buffer solution as the electrolyte. The in situ Raman samples of Ag NP and Ag NC were prepared on Ag foil. The electrode was encased in a PEEK fitting, with an exposed geometric surface area of 1 cm2. A platinum wire and an Ag/AgCl electrode (saturated KCl, Gaoss union) were used as the counter and the reference electrode, respectively. Electrochemical measurements were carried out with a potentiostat CompactStat.e20250, IVIUM. The Raman tests were performed on a Confocal Raman Microscopy (RENISHAW, inVia reflex) equipped with a 532 nm He-Ne laser. The signal acquisition time is 51 s for each Raman spectrum.

Calculation of local pH
Potassium phosphite (K2HPO4) is derived from phosphorous acid (H3PO3), a diprotic acid possessing only two acidic protons (pKa1 ≈ 1.3, pKa2 ≈ 6.7). Under strongly alkaline conditions (pH=11.0), the phosphite species exists almost entirely in its fully deprotonated form (HPO32–), far well outside its effective buffering range. As a result, the phosphite electrolyte provides negligible buffering capacity. Consequently, the local pH increase near the cathode is governed primarily by the generation and diffusion of OH– produced during electrochemical reactions. For the OH– generation flux, J OH–, each electron transferred at the cathode approximately produces one OH– ion. Therefore,

J OH– = i / F (6)

where i is the current density and F is the Faradic constant (96495 C mol–1).

One-dimensional steady-state diffusion balance model was adopted in this manuscript. Fast ion coupling (electroneutral diffusion) was assumed. Therefore,

J OH– = Deff (C Surface – C bulk) / δ

where the parameters could be used as 19: bulk pH=11.0, C bulk = 10–3 M; diffusion layer thickness δ=100 µm; Deff = 5.27 × 10–9 m2 s–1; pH Surface = 14 + log10 (C Surface).

Computational model
Ag(111) and Ag(100) surface was modeled by a (3√3×3√3)R30° supercell and a 6×5 supercell, respectively. All surface models were composed of 4 layers of atoms with 2 uppermost layers relaxed. The metal slabs were separated by a ~20 Å vacuum space. The Brillouin zone was sampled at a 3×3×1 k-point mesh with Γ-centered for hexagonal supercells and Monkhorst-Pack for orthorhombic supercells. The Gibbs free energy under ambient conditions was corrected using a computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model68.

DFT calculations
Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed utilizing the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) in conjunction with the projector augmented wave (PAW) method69,70. The revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE)71 exchange-correlation functional was applied, and the dispersion effects were accounted for by employing the semi-empirical D3 method72,73. For this method, the consideration of a Hubbard U parameter is typically not necessary. The cutoff energy was set to 450 eV. The convergence threshold of electronic and force was set to 10−6 eV atom–1 and 0.02 eV Å–1, respectively. The Methfessel-Paxton smearing was applied with a smearing width of 0.15 eV. Related information is attached in Supplementary Data 1.

Data availability
The data that support the findings of this study are available within the paper and supplementary information. Additional data are available from the corresponding author on request. Source data are provided with this paper.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, the authors reported an electrocatalytic system to synthesize amine from HMF and methylamine using Ag nanoparticles (denoted as Ag NPs). Although the Faraday efficiency and production rate are considerable, this reaction is not novel and extremely non-challenging. The most critical issue is that the C-N coupling reaction is likely to be a spontaneous reaction process, where the electrocatalyst mainly completes the hydrogenation reaction step, which conflicts with the proposed mechanism in this manuscript. As a result, we can not recommend that the current form of the manuscript be published on the Nature Communications. The following questions should be considered and be clearly reported:
1. Given the well-documented rapidity of amine-aldehyde condensation reactions under ambient conditions, a critical question arises regarding the authors' reported system containing concurrent HMF and methylamine: does the imine intermediate predominate in the reaction medium under these conditions? To conclusively address this mechanistic consideration, the authors should provide supporting evidence including (but not limited to) time-resolved 1H NMR spectroscopic characterization of the reaction mixture, complemented by comparative kinetic studies and/or mass spectrometric analysis of intermediate species.
2. A second mechanistic concern pertains to the potential influence of stoichiometric parameters. Specifically, the rationale for selecting the current methylamine/HMF molar ratio requires clarification. Have the authors systematically explored reactant stoichiometry optimization (e.g., elevated methylamine concentrations)? To substantiate the claimed catalytic specificity, control experiments comparing Faradaic efficiencies across (i) varied methylamine concentrations and (ii) different metal electrodes (including non-noble counterparts) should be supplemented, alongside detailed kinetic isotope effect analyses.
3. The obvious difference between Figure 4c and Figure 4d is puzzling. Even if there are differences in the dominant adsorption configurations on the catalyst surface, it does not mean that other adsorption configurations do not exist. However, we could not observe any signals around ~1024 cm-1 which could be attributed to the furan ring of C-H, we recommend that the authors clarify this issue clearly.
4. Given the established morphological sensitivity of electrocatalytic systems (e.g., Ag nanoparticles vs. nanocubes differentially exposing {111}/{100} facets), has rigorous morphological characterization (including crystallographic orientation and particle size distribution) been performed to ensure structural homogeneity across the metal electrodes in Figure S1? This is particularly critical as substrate-dependent variations in active site geometry and surface energy landscapes could artificially modulate Faradaic efficiency trends.
5. Computing energies of adsorbed species uses the harmonic approximation, which can be very sensitive to low-frequency modes. If the used cutoff is too small then the entropy of the adsorbate will be substantially over-estimated. The authors do compute the energy, and the many difference is only 0.2 eV, which is much close to the typical DFT error of ~0.2 eV, and this conclusion could easily change if a different functional or U value is used. In other words, it is not conclusive evidence.
6. Computational Refinement: Although the theoretical calculations align with experimental outcomes, they fail to rationalize the high selectivity toward MAMF. We suggest: (i) Incorporating energy profiles for methylamine’s nucleophilic attack on the aldehyde group to quantify activation barriers. (ii) Comparing energy differences between hydrogenation and nucleophilic pathways to elucidate competitive reaction dynamics.
7. Substrate Scope Expansion: Additional substrate screening experiments are necessary to validate the universality of their design strategy for aldehyde-based C–N coupling reactions. Testing structurally diverse aldehydes would clarify whether the observed mechanism is generalizable.
Minor: the widely accepted resolution of HRTEM is 0.01 nm. Please correct the statements in Figure 1b and Figure 1d. All spelling and grammar in the manuscript should be thoroughly checked, such as “0.205n m” in Figure 1d. The authors' work still has some font issues that need to be corrected. Italicize “in situ” (e.g., Line 6 of Conclusions). Replace hyphens with en dashes for chemical bonds (e.g., “C-N” → C–N in the SI).

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript reports on modulating the adsorption behavior of substrates by tailoring the surface structure of silver (Ag) catalysts, thereby significantly enhancing the electrochemical C–N coupling of biomass-derived 5-hydroxymethylfurfural (HMF) with methylamine to produce 5-[(methylamino)methyl]-2-furanmethanol (MAMF). The optimized Ag nanoparticles (NPs), predominantly exposing the (111) facet, exhibit an impressive Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 89.2% and a selectivity of 90.1% for C–N coupling at −0.45 V vs. RHE. This performance is among the best reported to date. Systematic in situ spectroscopic investigations combined with DFT calculations reveal that HMF adsorbs onto the Ag(111) surface in a distinct η¹(C)-aldehyde configuration. This specific adsorption mode increases the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon, facilitating C=O bond polarization and promoting nucleophilic attack by methylamine, thereby enhancing catalytic activity. Overall, this work offers a novel strategy for modulating reactant adsorption to achieve selective electrochemical organic synthesis. It holds the potential to inspire the development of high-performance electrocatalysts. I recommend the publication after revisions, as outlined in the following comments.
1.Since the Ag NPs and Ag NCs exhibit different morphologies, their electrochemically active surface areas are likely to differ, which could affect their catalytic performance. The authors are encouraged to provide ECSA data to clarify whether this factor plays a substantial role in the observed activity differences.
2.The effect of methylamine concentration on the reaction performance is not discussed. As the adsorption of methylamine may also influence the C-N coupling process, the authors should consider including a discussion or experimental results addressing this variable.
3.The manuscript presents charge-transfer resistance values derived from electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), but lacks information about the fitting procedure, including the equivalent circuit used and the associated standard errors. Providing these details would strengthen the credibility of the analysis.
4.The manuscript reports selectivity values, but does not clarify whether these are calculated based on carbon-containing products, nitrogen-containing products, or total product yield. The authors should explicitly state the basis for the selectivity calculation.
5.The authors present a comparison of linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) curves for the C-N coupling and HMF reduction reactions on Ag NPs (Supplementary Fig. 14). However, the corresponding data for Ag NCs are missing. Including this comparison would provide a more complete picture of the performance differences between the two catalysts.
6.Several key experimental procedures are insufficiently described. For instance, the rotary steaming step used before liquid product quantification (mentioned in Supplementary Fig. 11) is not included in the Methods section, and specific operating parameters are not provided. Additionally, variables used in Equations (2)-(6) are not clearly defined. The authors should revise the manuscript to address these omissions.
7.Error bars are absent in the Faradaic efficiency data presented in Fig. 3e,f. To demonstrate reproducibility and data reliability, the authors should include error bars.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript describes tailoring the surface structure of Ag catalysts to modulate HMF adsorption behavior significantly enhances C–N coupling selectivity. It presents a compelling study on facet-dependent C–N coupling but requires revisions to address methodological gaps, clarify mechanistic claims, and contextualize performance metrics. Following are some comments on this work.
1. The manuscript is generally well-structured, but the figures and schemes need clearer labeling. For example, Scheme I (page 3) is referenced but not included in the main text, which may confuse readers. Figure 2d and 2e are described as showing "potential-dependent production rate" and "stability tests," but the axes labels in the figure are unclear. Please ensure all axes and legends are explicitly defined.
2. The introduction lacks a focused discussion on recent advances in electrochemical C–N coupling, particularly for biomass-derived substrates. Highlighting specific challenges in HMF amination (e.g., overhydrogenation, dimerization) and how this work addresses them would sharpen the novelty.
3. While facet-dependent adsorption modulation is not novel, its application to electrochemical C-N coupling of HMF is innovative. However, the introduction lacks a critical comparison with recent works on similar systems (e.g., Cu or Pd catalysts for HMF upgrading). A table comparing FE/selectivity with prior studies would better contextualize the advancements.
4. The synthesis methods for Ag NP and Ag NC are well-documented, but the absence of TEM/SEM images in the main text (relegated to Supplementary Figs. 2–3) weakens the immediate validation of morphology. Key characterization data (e.g., lattice spacing, XRD peaks) should be highlighted in the main text. Stability tests over 10 cycles (Fig. 2e, f) are insufficient to claim long-term durability. Additional data (e.g., 24-hour chronoamperometry) would strengthen the practical relevance.
5. The authors attribute the high selectivity to η¹(C)-aldehyde adsorption but do not fully address how methylamine adsorption influences the reaction. Competitive adsorption between HMF and methylamine could alter pathways; this should be discussed. Product quantification relies on LC/GC, but potential intermediates (e.g., aldimine) are not tracked. Including time-dependent product distribution would clarify reaction kinetics.
6. The DFT calculations lack methodological details (e.g., functional, basis set, slab models). A brief description in the main text or Methods section should be provided for reproducibility.
7. The proposed mechanism assumes direct nucleophilic attack by methylamine on adsorbed HMF but does not address the role of protonation states or pH effects. Experiments varying pH could elucidate how proton availability impacts aldimine formation and reduction.
8. The manuscript does not consider potential surface reconstruction of Ag NPs/NCs under operating conditions. XPS or post-reaction TEM of used catalysts would verify structural stability and rule out facet restructuring during electrolysis. Competitive adsorption between HMF and methylamine is ignored. Surface coverage studies (e.g., via electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance) could clarify whether methylamine adsorption limits reaction rates.
9. The use of a three-electrode H-cell with a bipolar membrane may not reflect industrially relevant conditions. Testing in a flow cell or membrane electrode assembly (MEA) would better demonstrate scalability.
10. The environmental impact of using methylamine (a toxic reagent) is not addressed. Exploring greener amine sources (e.g., ammonia) or coupling with renewable NH₃ synthesis could enhance sustainability.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We sincerely thank the reviewer for the important comments. We have carefully revised this manuscript and improved the related details according to the insightful suggestions. Detailed responses to the comments are listed below.

Specific Comment R1-1: Given the well-documented rapidity of amine-aldehyde condensation reactions under ambient conditions, a critical question arises regarding the authors’ reported system containing concurrent HMF and methylamine: does the imine intermediate predominate in the reaction medium under these conditions? To conclusively address this mechanistic consideration, the authors should provide supporting evidence including (but not limited to) time-resolved 1H NMR spectroscopic characterization of the reaction mixture, complemented by comparative kinetic studies and/or mass spectrometric analysis of intermediate species.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. We agree that amine-aldehyde condensation reactions can proceed rapidly under certain conditions, particularly in anhydrous or acidic environments (Patai, S. (Ed.). The Chemistry of Carbon Nitrogen Double Bonds, 1970, John Wiley & Sons.). However, an aqueous phosphate buffer solution at pH 11 was used in our research. Under this specific condition, the equilibrium for imine formation can be less favorable or slower than commonly assumed, especially when competing with the hydrogenation of the aldehyde (ACS Catal., 2016, 6,1840). Therefore, imine intermediate should not predominate in the reaction medium. To support this idea, additional experiments were conducted.
According to the reviewer’s suggestion, time-resolved 1H NMR spectroscopic characterization of the reaction mixture was performed under operando electrochemical conditions. The results show that the imine content stays at a consistently low level throughout the electrochemical reaction with a general decreasing trend (Supplementary Fig. 19). This phenomenon suggests that the imine intermediate does not predominate in the reaction medium. Additionally, time-resolved Raman spectroscopy of the reaction solution without applied potential was collected (Fig. R1). The results show that the concentration of the imine intermediate remains constantly low in the bulk solution under non-electrochemical conditions, confirming that the equilibrium for reversible imine formation reaction is less favorable in this reaction condition.
Collectively, these results suggest that spontaneously formed imine intermediates in the bulk solution should not be the reason for the high production rate obtained in our study. Thus, the reductive coupling between HMF and methylamine is an electrocatalytic process that occurs at the surface of the electrode, with the adsorption behavior of the HMF molecule as one of the key influencing factors on the performance.
With the conclusion discussed above, a detailed kinetic study and mass spectrometric analysis of the key imine intermediate are important to further support the idea of adsorption-configuration-induced impact toward intermediate formation, as suggested by the reviewer. However, accurate quantification of the intermediates formed at the surface during the reaction is hard to realize in this study. Fortunately, the in situ Raman spectroscopy provides direct and compelling evidence to support the main idea of this work (Fig. 4c, d). The observed distinct spectral changes, particularly the redshift of the C=O stretching frequency of HMF adsorbed on Ag NP (Fig. 4c), unequivocally indicate a weakening and polarization of the carbonyl bond upon adsorption. This activation is precisely what enhances the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon and facilitates the subsequent nucleophilic attack by methylamine. The dramatic differences in product distribution and selectivity observed between Ag NP and Ag NC (Fig. 2b, c) further corroborate this surface-mediated activation. This distinct catalytic behavior strongly supports that the catalyst surface actively steers the reaction pathway by modulating HMF adsorption. Revisions of the manuscript are as follows:
Manuscript Lines 209-214.
Besides, time-resolved 1H NMR spectroscopic characterization of the reaction mixture was performed under operando electrochemical conditions (Supplementary Fig. 19). The result shows that the imine content stays at a consistently low level throughout the electrochemical reaction with a general decreasing trend, suggesting the reductive coupling between HMF and methylamine is an electrocatalytic process that occurs at the surface of the electrode.
SI Lines 161-164:
Supplementary Fig. 19. Time-resolved 1H NMR for the electrolyte during the C–N coupling on Ag NP with (a) 5, (b) 10, (c) 20, (d) 40, and (e) 60 C charge passed. (f) The concentration of imine as the amount of charge passed.
Fig. R1. Time-resolved Raman spectra of the electrolyte without electrocatalytic reaction.

Specific Comment R1-2: A second mechanistic concern pertains to the potential influence of stoichiometric parameters. Specifically, the rationale for selecting the current methylamine/HMF molar ratio requires clarification. Have the authors systematically explored reactant stoichiometry optimization (e.g., elevated methylamine concentrations)? To substantiate the claimed catalytic specificity, control experiments comparing Faradaic efficiencies across (i) varied methylamine concentrations and (ii) different metal electrodes (including non-noble counterparts) should be supplemented, alongside detailed kinetic isotope effect analyses.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comments. We have systematically explored the influence of methylamine concentration on the electrochemical C–N coupling reaction. Our results identified 1000 mM as the optimal methylamine concentration (Supplementary Fig. 12).
Regarding control experiments with different metal electrodes, we have performed a comprehensive comparison. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 1, we evaluated various commercial metal foils (Fe, Ni, Cu, Pt, Zn, Sn, Ag, Cd, and In) for the electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF with methylamine. These initial screening experiments clearly demonstrated that Ag exhibits exceptional electrocatalytic performance, achieving the highest partial current density and Faradaic efficiency for MAMF production among the tested metals. This superior performance was attributed to the moderate HMF adsorption strength on Ag, which is a critical finding that guided our subsequent in-depth study focusing on facet-controlled Ag catalysts and their impact on the adsorption configuration of the substrate.
Furthermore, we have conducted kinetic isotope effect (KIE) analyses on the Ag NP catalyst, as presented in Fig. 3d. The observed cathodic shift of 145 mV when replacing H O with D O strongly indicates that a proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) step is essential for the C–N coupling reaction. Specific Comment R1-3: The obvious difference between Figure 4c and Figure 4d is puzzling. Even if there are differences in the dominant adsorption configurations on the catalyst surface, it does not mean that other adsorption configurations do not exist. However, we could not observe any signals around ~1024 cm–1 which could be attributed to the furan ring of C-H, we recommend that the authors clarify this issue clearly.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful comments. The distinct differences between the in situ Raman spectra of Ag NP (Fig. 4c) and Ag NC (Fig. 4d) are important and serve as direct spectroscopic evidence supporting our proposed facet-dependent adsorption configurations of HMF. As stated in our manuscript, for Ag NP, the peak at 1022 cm–1 is consistently observed and attributed to the C–H stretching of the furan ring (Fig. 4a). This spectral feature is indicative of the η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration, where the furan ring adopts a horizontally tilted orientation relative to the catalyst surface, allowing for the detection of its C–H vibrations. This peak remains visible across the investigated potential range in Fig. 4c. In contrast, for Ag NC, the Raman spectra (Fig. 4d) exhibit a prominent peak at 1002 cm–1, which we attribute to the hydroxymethyl group, and the appearance of a peak at 718 cm–1 corresponding to the C–O–C stretching of the furan ring. Concurrently, the furan ring C–H stretching peak around ~1022/1024 cm–1 is indeed absent or significantly diminished on Ag NC. This distinct spectral profile on Ag NC strongly supports the η2(C,O)-aldehyde adsorption configuration. In this mode, the C–O–C end of the furan ring, along with the hydroxymethyl group, interacts more closely with the catalyst surface. This different orientation of the furan ring, where it is less horizontally oriented or more directly interacting through its oxygen-containing functionalities, would naturally lead to a reduced signal from the furan ring C–H stretching, as its vibrational mode might be less enhanced by surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS) or its orientation is less favorable for detection compared to other interacting groups.
While it is plausible that other minor adsorption configurations might coexist, the dominant and distinct adsorption modes on Ag NP and Ag NC, as unequivocally evidenced by these clear and reproducible spectroscopic differences, are responsible for dictating the observed dramatic differences in reaction selectivity. The consistent correlation between these unique spectral fingerprints and the vastly different product distributions (high MAMF selectivity on Ag NP vs. favoring BHMF/BHH on Ag NC) strongly supports our conclusion that the adsorption configuration is the critical factor steering the reaction pathway. Specific Comment R1-4: Given the established morphological sensitivity of electrocatalytic systems (e.g., Ag nanoparticles vs. nanocubes differentially exposing {111}/{100} facets), has rigorous morphological characterization (including crystallographic orientation and particle size distribution) been performed to ensure structural homogeneity across the metal electrodes in Figure S1? We would like to clarify that the data presented in Supplementary Figure 1 corresponds to the initial screening experiments conducted using commercial bulk metal foils (Fe, Ni, Cu, Pt, Zn, Sn, Ag, Cd, and In), not synthesized nanoparticles. Therefore, concerns regarding particle size distribution are not applicable to this specific set of experiments. While we acknowledge that the surface of commercial metal foils may exhibit a distribution of crystallographic orientations, the primary purpose of this initial screening was to identify a metal with moderate HMF interaction strength as a promising candidate for selective C–N coupling. The data demonstrated the outperforming performance of Ag among these bulk materials.
For the Ag NP and Ag NC catalysts, which are the model catalysts of interest, we have indeed performed rigorous and comprehensive morphological and crystallographic characterizations, as shown in Fig. 1 of the main manuscript. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images, corresponding fast Fourier transform (FFT) patterns, and X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (Fig. 1b, d, e) conclusively demonstrate that Ag NP predominantly exposes the (111) crystallographic plane, while Ag NC primarily exposes the (100) facet. Additionally, we also conducted characterization of catalysts after reactions (Supplementary Figs. 16–17). These results confirm the stability of Ag NP and Ag NC, demonstrating no significant facet reconstruction and consistent exposed facets throughout the reaction. This meticulous control and thorough characterization of exposed facets were paramount to our investigation of facet-dependent adsorption configurations and their impact on selectivity, which is the central theme and novelty of this manuscript. Specific Comment R1-5: Computing energies of adsorbed species uses the harmonic approximation, which can be very sensitive to low-frequency modes. If the used cutoff is too small then the entropy of the adsorbate will be substantially over-estimated. The authors do compute the energy, and the many difference is only 0.2 eV, which is much close to the typical DFT error of ~0.2 eV, and this conclusion could easily change if a different functional or U value is used. In other words, it is not conclusive evidence.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the helpful comments. We fully agree with the inherent limitations of the harmonic approximation, particularly concerning its potential sensitivity to low-frequency modes and the estimation of adsorbate entropy. Therefore, we verified our evidence in four aspects: (1) The adsorption energies of HMF on the (100) and (111) surfaces obtained from Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations (ΔE ) are -1.86 eV and -1.68 eV, respectively, DFT with a difference of 0.18 eV, which is the main contributor to the variation of ~ 0.20 eV in adsorption energy rather than the entropy parts. (2) We calculated the contribution of each vibrational mode to the entropy for the adsorbed HMF on both surfaces (Table R1). For vibrations with a wave number below 50 cm-1, whether treated as 50 cm-1 or ignored, the energy difference of T S between HMF* on the (100) and (111) surfaces does not exceed 0.07 eV. The contribution of computed entropy to the difference in adsorption energy is negligible. (3) To rule out the influ⋅ence of different functionals on the results, we further repeat our computation using the PBE functional, and the adsorption energies on the (100) and (111) surfaces are calculated to be -1.94 eV and -1.79 eV, respectively, with a difference of approximately 0.15 eV. It is worth noting that for metallic catalysts like Ag, the consideration of a Hubbard U parameter is typically not necessary, as electron localization issues that necessitate its use are generally absent. (4) We repeated the calculations at different adsorption sites five times, and the standard deviations of the adsorption energies on the (100) and (111) surfaces were 0.03 eV and 0.01 eV, respectively, ensuring the robustness and statistical significance of our calculated adsorption energies. It clearly indicates that η2(C,O)-aldehyde configuration leads to excessive adsorption of HMF, which promotes direct hydrogenation to form BHMF and BHH (Fig. 4b). The explanation of this section and our revision of the manuscript are as follows:

Specific Comment R1-7: Substrate Scope Expansion: Additional substrate screening experiments are necessary to validate the universality of their design strategy for aldehyde-based C–N coupling reactions. Testing structurally diverse aldehydes would clarify whether the observed mechanism is generalizable.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable comments. The study of the reaction between HMF and methylamine was driven by the high added value of its corresponding amine product, 5-[(methylamino)methyl]-2-furanmethanol (MAMF), which serves as a key chemical for the synthesis of the pharmaceutical Ranitidine. This consideration was stated in the Introduction section.
While we acknowledge the high utility and value of other aldehyde-based C–N coupling reactions, the current work focuses on the fundamental mechanistic insights of adsorption engineering of reactants for selective C–N coupling. Our findings establish that controlling the HMF adsorption mode (η1(C)-aldehyde vs. η2(C,O)-aldehyde) is critical for favoring C–N coupling. We believe tuning the absorption behavior should be a universal strategy for promoting heterogeneous electrochemical C–N coupling reactions. However, this universality might not be proved by testing the catalytic performance using the Ag NP and Ag NC catalysts in this work with varied aldehyde or amine substrates. The adsorption configuration tuning should be achieved by specifically designing the electrocatalyst for the target substrate. For a reaction of interest, we need to analyze the features of the substrate molecule (such as the existence of aromatic ring, the length of the alkyl chain, etc) to guide the fabrication of a specific catalyst structure, which requires a series of systematic investigations. Such a proof might be out of the scope of our current work. We will conduct related studies to further verify the effectiveness of adsorption tuning for electrochemical organic synthesis. To emphasize this point, we have added the related discussion on the future direction in the revised manuscript.

Specific Comment R3-2: The introduction lacks a focused discussion on recent advances in electrochemical C–N coupling, particularly for biomass-derived substrates. Highlighting specific challenges in HMF amination (e.g., overhydrogenation, dimerization) and how this work addresses them would sharpen the novelty.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the instructive comments. In the Introduction, we have summarized the current challenges of low selectivity and their underlying causes, primarily stemming from competing side reactions like C=O hydrogenation and C–C dimerization. We then introduce the specific work that addresses these problems through the analysis of the reaction mechanism. The subsequent paragraph further elucidates our strategy for tackling this issue, focusing on precise adsorption configuration modulation. Corresponding revisions of the manuscript are as follows:
Manuscript Lines 59-76:
Many electrocatalysts have been investigated for this reaction (Pt, Cu, Sn, Zn, and Ag).9,11
However, a lack of rational catalyst design has resulted in the easy occurrence of side reactions and low selectivity of C–N coupling12,13. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that promoting the nucleophilic attack step is crucial for effectively enhancing the overall selectivity of C–N coupling reactions11,14. Taking the electrochemical C–N coupling of HMF and methylamine as an example, the reaction pathway involves multiple steps (Scheme 1).3,11 Typically, HMF can be activated by the catalyst, forming the absorbed HMF (HMF*).9,15 Then, the target product MAMF is synthesized through two key steps16-18: (1) nucleophilic addition reaction of methylamine with the carbonyl group of HMF* to form the aldimine intermediate, and (2) subsequent reduction of the aldimine with protons from the electrolyte and electrons from the electrode to produce the MAMF (Scheme 1a). However, the hydrogenation and dimerization of HMF compete with the desired C–N coupling reaction to form 2,5-bis(hydroxymethyl)furan (BHMF) and bis(hydroxymethyl)hydrofuroin (BHH), respectively, leading to low selectivity (Scheme 1b, c).19-21 Therefore, precisely modulating the reactivity of the target aldehyde carbonyl group to facilitate nucleophilic attack becomes a key strategy for improving the selectivity of electrochemical C–N coupling.

Specific Comment R3-5: The authors attribute the high selectivity to η¹(C)-aldehyde adsorption but do not fully address how methylamine adsorption influences the reaction. Response: We thank the reviewer for the significant comments. We have systematically optimized the methylamine concentration to 1000 mM, ensuring an abundant supply of the nucleophile. Furthermore, our in situ Raman control experiments (Supplementary Figure 21) clearly show the characteristic peaks of methylamine, indicating its stable and sufficient adsorption on the catalyst surface under reaction conditions.
Regarding the tracking of potential intermediates like aldimine, we have performed time-resolved 1H NMR spectroscopic characterization of the reaction mixture under operando electrochemical conditions. The results show that the imine content stays at a consistently low level throughout the electrochemical reaction with a general decreasing trend (Supplementary Fig. 19). This observation indicates that relying solely on spontaneously formed imine intermediates in the bulk solution is insufficient to account for the observed product formation rate and consumption during the electrochemical process. The η1(C)-aldehyde adsorption configuration of HMF on Ag NP appropriately promotes the polarization of the C=O bond, thereby facilitating the nucleophilic attack by methylamine and enhancing the overall selectivity of the C–N coupling reaction. The dramatic differences in product distribution and selectivity observed between Ag NP and Ag NC (Fig. 2b, c) further corroborate this surface-mediated activation. This distinct catalytic behavior strongly supports that the catalyst surface actively steers the reaction pathway by modulating HMF adsorption. Density functional theory methods. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed utilizing the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP) in conjunction with the projector augmented wave (PAW) method.1, 2 The revised Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (RPBE)3 exchange-correlation functional was applied and the dispersion effects were accounted by employing semi-empirical D3 method.4, 5 For this method, the consideration of a Hubbard U parameter is typically not necessary. The cutoff energy was set to 450 eV. The convergence threshold of electronic and force was set to 10−6 eV atom–1 and 0.02 eV Å–1, respectively. Computational model. Ag(111) and Ag(100) surface was modeled by a (3√3×3√3)R30° supercell and a 6×5 supercell, respectively. All surface models were composed of 4 layers atoms with 2 uppermost layers relaxed. The metal slabs were separated by a ~20 Å vacuum space. The Brillouin zone was sampled at a 3×3×1 k-point mesh with Γ-centered for hexagonal supercells and Monkhorst Pack for orthorhombic supercells. The Gibbs free energy under ambient conditions was corrected using a computational hydrogen electrode (CHE) model.6

Specific Comment R3-7: The proposed mechanism assumes direct nucleophilic attack by methylamine on adsorbed HMF but does not address the role of protonation states or pH effects. Experiments varying pH could elucidate how proton availability impacts aldimine formation and reduction.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive comments. We chose pH 11 for the reaction electrolyte because at this pH (which is above the pKa of methylamine, ~10.6), a significant portion of methylamine is present in its neutral, nucleophilic form (CH NH ), which is essential for its efficient nucleophilic attack on the HMF carbonyl group to form the aldimine intermediate. This optimized pH condition ensures the availability of the active nucleophile.
Furthermore, our kinetic isotope effect (KIE) studies (Fig. 3d) provide direct evidence for the involvement of protons in the reaction mechanism. The observed cathodic shift of 145 mV upon switching from H O to D O strongly indicates that a proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) step is significant for the C–N coupling reaction. This confirms the important role of proton dynamics in the reduction of the aldimine intermediate and the overall C–N bond formation, thus addressing the involvement of proton availability in our proposed inner-sphere mechanism.
While systematic experiments varying pH across a wider range could indeed provide further detailed insights into how proton availability specifically impacts aldimine formation and subsequent reduction, our current study primarily focuses on elucidating the pivotal role of HMF adsorption configurations in steering reaction selectivity at an optimized pH. Exploring the full pH dependence is a valuable and logical direction for future research to further refine the understanding of the complex interplay between surface adsorption, electron transfer, and proton dynamics. The explanation of this section and our revision of the manuscript are as follows:

Specific Comment R3-8: The manuscript does not consider potential surface reconstruction of Ag NPs/NCs under operating conditions. XPS or post-reaction TEM of used catalysts would verify structural stability and rule out facet restructuring during electrolysis. Competitive adsorption between HMF and methylamine is ignored. Surface coverage studies (e.g., via electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance) could clarify whether methylamine adsorption limits reaction rates.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the important comments. Regarding potential surface reconstruction of Ag NP/NC under operating conditions, we have addressed this critical aspect with abundant experiments. As detailed in the “Result and Discussion” section and supported by Supplementary Figures 16–17, we performed post-reaction morphological and crystallographic characterization (TEM and XRD) of the used catalysts after 10 cycles of electrolysis. These results conclusively demonstrate that the morphology and crystal structure, including the predominant exposed facets, of both Ag NP and Ag NC remain almost unchanged. This robust structural stability under operando conditions ensures that the observed facet-dependent catalytic performance and selectivity are genuinely attributable to the intrinsic properties of the as-synthesized crystal facets rather than dynamic reconstruction.
Additionally, regarding the competitive adsorption behavior of substrates, our systematic optimization of methylamine concentration (to 1000 mM) ensures its abundant supply, and in situ Raman spectroscopy (Supplementary Figure 21, response to Specific Comment R3-5) confirms its stable adsorption on the catalyst surface. Furthermore, our HMF concentration dependence study (Figure 3f) indicates that HMF adsorption is a key limiting factor at lower concentrations, following Langmuir-Hinshelwood kinetics. These findings collectively suggest that under our optimized conditions, methylamine adsorption is not the rate-limiting step, and the primary kinetic and selectivity control stems from the activation and adsorption configuration of HMF. While techniques like electrochemical quartz crystal microbalance (EQCM) could offer further quantitative insights into surface coverage, we could not conduct this experiment due to the limitations of the resources. It would be a valuable direction for more in-depth kinetic studies in the future, building upon the fundamental mechanistic understanding established in this work.

Specific Comment R3-9: The use of a three-electrode H-cell with a bipolar membrane may not reflect industrially relevant conditions. Testing in a flow cell or membrane electrode assembly (MEA) would better demonstrate scalability.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the beneficial comments. We agree with the reviewer that a three-electrode H-cell setup may not directly reflect industrially relevant conditions or demonstrate immediate scalability. However, it is important to emphasize that the primary objective of this fundamental research is to elucidate the intricate reaction mechanism of electrochemical C–N coupling, particularly the pivotal role of substrate adsorption configurations. Indeed, we have already performed preliminary investigations into the electrocatalytic C–N coupling reaction in a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) setup, utilizing the same reaction conditions but at higher HMF substrate concentrations (Fig. R2a). Our activity test results from the MEA system indicate a significant enhancement in reaction current and rate, primarily due to the reduced resistance afforded by the thin liquid film within the MEA, which effectively lowers the ohmic drop (Fig. R2b). However, we observed a decrease in reaction selectivity under these high substrate concentration conditions in the MEA, which we attribute to limitations in the current catalyst design when operating at such elevated concentrations and current densities.
This observation highlights a new set of challenges that require further catalyst engineering specific to MEA operation. Consequently, we have dedicated another work (Chem. Eng. Sci., 317, 122039) specifically to the study of electrocatalytic C–N coupling reactions within membrane electrode reactors. In that work, we are focusing on introducing modifications, such as the incorporation of Ru, to enhance the adsorption and activation of imine intermediates, thereby aiming to establish a robust electrocatalytic C–N coupling system capable of operating efficiently under high substrate concentrations and high current densities (Fig R2c). Therefore, while demonstrating scalability in MEA is undoubtedly crucial for the eventual practical application, the current manuscript remains focused on providing the fundamental mechanistic understanding of adsorption engineering in the H-cell, which serves as the essential groundwork for future advancements in MEA-based systems. Our subsequent work directly addresses the scalability and high-concentration challenges in MEA, building upon the mechanistic insights gained from this study. We have added the related discussion on the future direction in the revised manuscript.

Specific Comment R3-10: The environmental impact of using methylamine (a toxic reagent) is not addressed. Exploring greener amine sources (e.g., ammonia) or coupling with renewable NH₃ synthesis could enhance sustainability.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the meaningful comments. Our selection of methylamine as the nitrogen source in this study was primarily driven by the high added value of the target product, 5-[(methylamino)methyl]-2-furanmethanol (MAMF), which is a key intermediate for the synthesis of the pharmaceutical Ranitidine. This specific application highlights a direct pathway to a high-value chemical from biomass. Our current work focuses on establishing the fundamental mechanistic principles of adsorption engineering for selective C–N coupling. While exploring greener and more sustainable amine sources, such as aqueous ammonia or even coupling with electrochemical ammonia synthesis from renewable feedstocks, represents a highly significant and promising direction for future research. A key challenge with using ammonia as an N source is the difficulty in selectively obtaining specific primary or secondary amine products. This would undoubtedly enhance the overall sustainability profile of electrochemical C–N coupling processes, and is a direction we are committed to investigating in our future work. We have added the related discussion on the future direction in the revised manuscript.
